newsitem.title: USA: Sep foreign crude offers roll into US, buyers wary.
newsitem.headline: Sep foreign crude offers roll into US, buyers wary.

text.p: September foreign crude offers quietly began rolling into the U.S. Gulf Coast on Tuesday, but buyers remained hesitant ahead of renewed Iraqi oil sales, traders said.
Activity was generally subdued. "Everybody's calling everybody with nothing to say," a Gulf Coast refiner said.
Three companies continued to test the waters for Brent interest in mid-September, asking around 25 cents a barrel under September West Texas Intermediate/Cushing on a delivered basis, traders said.
The September spread between WTI and Brent was around $1.20-1.30 a barrel on Tuesday afternoon, down about 10 cents from Monday.
Two Dated Brent cargoes changed hands in London at August Brent plus two cents and August Brent plus four cents, marking a slight recovery from late last week, traders said.
U.S. buyers remained skeptical. "I don't know how serious they are because of the arb," a Gulf Coast refiner said.

Among other September offerings, a pair of trading companies were each offering Nigerian Qua Iboe for September 1-5 and September 7-11 arrival. Each seller was asking around $1.90 a barrel over Dated Brent, traders said.
Two trading houses were also offering Argentine Santa Cruz for September 8-10 and September 15-20, asking around WTI plus 25 cents a barrel.
Colombian state oil company Ecopetrol was soliciting bids for Cano Limon, loading August 26-31, and South Blend, loading around August 20-30. Bids are due on Thursday, traders said.
Elsewhere in Latin America, Chile's state oil refiner Empresa Nacional del Petroleo (ENAP) was seeking to buy 960,000 barrels of crude for September 16-20 arrival.
Bids are due on July 31.
Chile normally buys a combination of Ecuadoran Oriente crude and a West African grade such as Palanca.
Meanwhile, a few cargoes of Nigerian crude were still looking for homes in the second half of August, traders said.
Qua Iboe and Bonny Light were on offer around Dated Brent plus $1.80 a barrel, while Brass River was around $1.95 a barrel.
Buying and selling was backed up, traders said, amid continued uncertainty over the timing of renewed Iraqi humanitarian exports.
A spokesman for the United Nations said on Monday that its review of Iraqi's aid distribution plan under the "oil-for-food" program can be completed by the end of the week.

Under the "oil-for-food" agreement, which first took effect last December 10, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months to buy humanitarian goods to offset the effects of snactions in place since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The program was renewed beginning June 8, but Iraq has yet to restart oil sales pending U.N. approval of its latest aid distribution plan.
Iraq had been hoping the latest six-month period would not start until the plan was approved, but the U.N. Security Council insists the clock began ticking on June 8.
This means that Baghdad has until September 5 to market the first $1 billion of oil allowed during each 90-day period.
Traders say that translates into 1.5 million to two million barrels per day (bpd) of oil once sales get underway, perhaps around mid-August.
--Patricia Garip-Bertuol NY Energy Desk ((+1 212 859 1620))
